title: Microgrid Manager
headline: From power readings to useful decisions.
summary: I led the design of three BiLSTMs and a distributed energy pipeline: 0.932 heat-pump F1 on held-out physics-labeled data, with single-digit-ms ONNX inference per panel.
label: local appliance inference
problem: A solar home produces continuous telemetry. Its operator needs a clearer answer: which appliances are running, how the energy system is behaving and what to do next. I led the UCSC capstone that brought those readings into a local inference and monitoring system.
approach: As lead engineer, I designed and trained three two-layer PyTorch BiLSTMs with appliance-specific heads and weighted loss. Physics-informed labeling captured sustained loads, compressor cycles, high-power events and paired pulse patterns.

I engineered the deployment contract around each ONNX model: feature normalization, appliance names and thresholds travel with the graph. Independent output probabilities allow several appliances to run at once.

I connected Kafka and MQTT telemetry through three EdgeLake / AnyLog nodes and PostgreSQL to ONNX inference, FastAPI and React dashboards. Load, Generation, Storage and Decision Support organize the system around the operator’s decisions.
I coordinated model, labeling and dashboard delivery with weekly sponsor reviews, working with Dr. Pat Mantey and the AnyLog team on infrastructure.
result: The BiLSTM work achieved 0.932 heat-pump F1 on held-out physics-labeled data.

The distributed pipeline handles roughly 960 messages/min across three nodes. The published LF Edge report records single-digit milliseconds of CPU inference per panel, with predictions written every 30 seconds.

Delivered local inference across three panels and a residential monitoring dashboard; completed the capstone in October 2026. All 11 solar-path tests passed locally and inside the deployed inference container.
Co-authored the LF Edge article documenting the residential edge-intelligence system.
note: Rule-derived evaluation is not independent appliance accuracy. Rare loads still need broader ground-truth coverage; fully automated appliance control was outside the completed capstone scope.
technical: Model outputs are independent appliance probabilities, allowing multiple loads to be ON at once. Physics-informed rules add temporal and power constraints; ambiguous windows are excluded instead of forced into training labels.

A model deployment couples the ONNX graph with feature normalization, appliance names and thresholds. Checking those contracts prevents a numerically valid output vector from being interpreted against the wrong labels.
Kafka / MQTT → EdgeLake / AnyLog → PostgreSQL → ONNX + rules → FastAPI → dashboard. I kept the interface and inference layers separate so a GUI change did not create a second model runtime.

The deployment runs as roughly 11 Docker containers, brought up with a single docker compose command. Keeping ingestion, inference, storage and presentation services separate makes the operational boundaries explicit.

The Ask feature connects a local model through Ollama to an MCP client exposing 18 tools. It gives the dashboard a natural-language interface while keeping the local inference path separate from language-model responses.

Evaluation scope: 0.932 heat-pump F1 is measured against held-out physics-derived labels. Only two of 22 appliance outputs had independent measurement in the capstone; automated appliance control was outside its completed scope.

implementation.use: Train appliance models and run local inference.
Move meter readings into queryable storage.
Expose readings, predictions and a local question interface.

takeaway: The product is the complete path from a meter reading to a useful decision. Explicit model contracts, local inference and clear service boundaries make that path maintainable.

title: GX10 Microgrid Intelligence — Hackathon
headline: More intelligence. On one machine.
summary: Local Nemotron inference and GPU-trained forecasts on one GX10. Built for the hack.dev UCSC AI hackathon; reached 91.91% held-out agreement with the BiLSTM teacher.
label: held-out agreement with the teacher
problem: The hack.dev UCSC AI hackathon was an opportunity to extend Microgrid Manager from monitoring into local reasoning and forecasting. I brought training, inference and data services together on the GX10 while keeping each prediction tied to an explicit data and model contract.
approach: I deployed the stack on the GX10’s Grace Blackwell platform: GB10 GPU training, ARM-compatible data services and local serving. Recorded meter data enabled a self-contained event demo; read-only meter and solar collection later added direct-source inputs.
I built the physics-labeling and rolling walk-forward training path for panel-specific BiLSTMs, preserving an 18-feature normalization contract and calibrated ONNX exports.

I distilled the gated BiLSTM into Nemotron 3.5 Lightning with rank-16 LoRA. Each round merges the adapter, scores held-out windows and refreshes a fixed-size training replay buffer. The live Q8_0 model serves through llama.cpp with per-head BiLSTM fallback.

I separated question answering from appliance inference: Ollama serves the reasoning interface, while the fine-tuned model produces structured appliance states. The system map combines verified deployment topology with separately labeled extracted relationships.

For power forecasts, I compared TiDE-inspired PyTorch, CUDA XGBoost, seasonal baselines and blends using meter history, weather and missingness flags. Versioned models and an atomic champion pointer let retraining proceed while serving continues.
result: Reached 91.91% held-out agreement with the gated BiLSTM teacher on 300 validation windows, up from 82.14% in the first round.
Deployed the quantized local NILM engine with per-head fallback. Q8_0 matched the merged BF16 model on 166 of 176 head decisions in the recorded comparison.
Built a forecasting dataset from more than 30.7 million deduplicated meter records across 16 channels and roughly 977,000 solar records, with coverage filters that preserve missing intervals.

Added prediction and system-map views with minute-level forecast refresh and 15-minute forecast origins. Model promotion requires at least 1% improvement in normalized MAE on shared validation origins.
takeaway: Model training and live serving share one machine, so versioning and promotion rules are part of the model design. Separating appliance states, forecasts and conversational answers gives each output a clear job and evaluation.
technical: The NILM input contract uses 100 × 18 windows. The teacher target includes the same mutual-exclusion and power gates used in serving, rather than copying raw recall-biased network outputs. Hard-example mining draws from training data, never the held-out validation split.

Forecast selection, empirical interval calibration and final testing use three disjoint 14-day blocks. Training windows cannot cross split boundaries, and normalization is fitted only on training data. Historical weather inputs use previously issued forecasts rather than realized future observations.

Prediction intervals come from calibration residuals per channel and horizon. Reported test coverage can fall below the nominal 80%, so the dashboard exposes observed coverage rather than promising certainty.

Forecasts require sufficient recent source coverage. Replay timestamps do not count as new live data for retraining, missing measured PV can withhold the solar baseline, and later direct-source collection provides provenance without Docker-control permissions.

Local training, model serving and data services share the GX10 memory pool. I separated model evaluation, merge, quantization and serving stages, retained model backups and fixed export handling so external ONNX weight files were not silently omitted from deployment.

The 91.91% result measures distillation agreement with the gated BiLSTM teacher on 300 held-out windows. It is not independent, submetered appliance accuracy. The recorded deployment used six-hour retraining checks; candidate promotion preserves the current serving model when the required improvement is not met.

implementation.use: Create weighted training labels, fit panel models with walk-forward validation and preserve the feature/head contract at deployment.
Distill gated appliance decisions into a local model, retain BiLSTM fallback and serve a separate reasoning interface.
Compare multi-horizon candidates, calibrate intervals and promote versioned models only after validation improves.

title: Silicon Performance Lab
headline: 11.2× the throughput. Proven on hardware.
summary: An asynchronous C++ runtime delivered 11.2× higher throughput on a physical FPGA: 702 jobs/s across 12,000 validated jobs, alongside custom graphics and compute hardware.
label: SPL2 jobs validated on hardware
problem: Performance work needs a repeatable workload, a verified answer and a clean measurement interval. I built a lab that connects those three across Apple Core ML, FPGA graphics and a custom host/device runtime.
approach: I built SPL2, a C++17 asynchronous runtime with futures and up to 16 outstanding jobs. CRC-protected UART frames, request epochs, credit-based flow control and watchdog recovery coordinate the host and FPGA.
I implemented banked vectors and 1/2/4/8-lane dot-product and XOR-reduction kernels. Timing sweeps selected eight lanes at 30 MHz.

In a separate graphics image, I built integer compute lanes, BRAM transfers and a Verilog triangle rasterizer. A 64×64 framebuffer feeds independent 640×480 RGB444 DVI scanout; UART supports commands and framebuffer readback.

I validated raster pixels against a software reference, simulated a complete frame, then synthesized, routed and exercised the physical iCEBreaker. The UART runner records cycle counts and host latency for every checked transaction.

I wrote a Swift Core ML runner for a deterministic four-layer convolution workload and a JavaScript / Node.js dashboard for controls, latency charts and exports. Five warmups and three 50-prediction trials separate execution timing from compilation, loading and output checks.
result: Validated 12,000 SPL2 jobs on the physical iCEBreaker. A 10,000-job run at queue depth 16 sustained 702.266 jobs/s versus 62.5021 at depth 1—an 11.2× throughput improvement.
Eight lanes complete a 256-pair dot product or XOR reduction in 35 device cycles versus 259 with one lane: 7.4× fewer cycles. At 30 MHz, the device calculation takes 1.167 microseconds.

The selected image uses 3,835 of 5,280 logic cells, all 30 RAM blocks and all eight DSP blocks; routed timing reached 31.219 MHz. Three invalid-vector requests were rejected and followed by successful epoch recoveries.

The separate graphics image passed 2,113 physical transactions: 938 compute, 938 memory and 237 raster runs. The external monitor displayed the rendered triangle; simulation checked 420,000 pixel periods.
The saved M4 experiment measured 0.154 ms median CPU-only prediction latency and 0.139 ms for CPU + Neural Engine, with all 131,072 output elements checked against the CPU reference.
Passed 13 dashboard/server and data-contract tests plus eight host-protocol and power-integration tests.
takeaway: Keeping work in flight raised throughput 11.2×; adding lanes cut device cycles 7.4×. Measuring both identifies the next optimization target: transport and host overhead.
technical: SPL2 is a separate compute-only image; it does not include the earlier DVI rasterizer. The October 25 graphics results and October 29 SPL2 results describe different bitstreams. UART simulation reached about 2,965 jobs/s; physical hardware measured 702 jobs/s. The physical 80%-of-link-ceiling target remains unmet.

Core ML compute policies allow CPU fallback. Preferred-device information is scheduling evidence, so I do not treat it as a trace proving which accelerator executed every operation. The saved run was taken on battery power; repeated independent runs on AC power would support stronger comparisons.

Video scanout runs independently of the UART request path. Hardware returned the expected 4,096 raster cycles and framebuffer pixels; configured-clock throughput is distinct from host round-trip timing. The repeated serial test does not saturate the compute engine or measure maximum board power.
The FPGA is fixed-function graphics hardware. It renders a fixed triangle and supports defined compute and memory exercises; it is not a general shader processor.

Energy analysis requires measured power covering the same interval as completed work. The integration code is tested, while physical watts, joules and work-per-joule measurements remain future experiments.

The 702 jobs/s result comes from a roughly 15-second sustained run, not long-duration qualification. The physical link reached 22.5% of its ideal response ceiling. Timing sweeps excluded a 36 MHz candidate that did not meet timing.

implementation.use: Time synchronous predictions under four compute policies and validate the complete output tensor.
Build separate DVI graphics and SPL2 compute images; bank resident vectors across eight lanes and verify timing on the UP5K.
Queue asynchronous work, validate framed replies and recovery, expose experiments, and retain reproducible benchmark evidence.

note: SPL2 hardware results recorded October 29, 2026; earlier DVI results recorded October 25. Animation is schematic, not a recording or timing scale. No watts, joules or performance-per-watt measurements are claimed. Source repository is private; GitHub access is required.

title: Linux GPU Power-Management Driver Lab
headline: Performance changes. Control stays intact.
summary: A Linux driver that coordinates four performance states and recovers from injected faults. Validated 400 concurrent sysfs requests in an ARM64 QEMU guest.
label: concurrent sysfs requests validated
problem: A performance-state change must coordinate voltage, frequency and concurrent callers. I built a Linux driver and emulated controller that make the transition, completion and recovery rules executable.
approach: I defined a shared C register-level model with four synthetic P-states, power-budget admission, thermal constraints, write-one-to-clear interrupt status and injectable faults. On a boost, voltage rises before frequency; on a downshift, frequency falls before voltage.

I implemented a Linux platform driver with a transaction mutex for request ownership and an IRQ-safe spinlock for register access. Delayed work advances the controller, a software IRQ handler acknowledges completion, and sysfs exposes controls and status to a C CLI.

I designed timeout recovery to drain outstanding work before reusing a completion. Terminal status can recover a lost notification; a still-busy controller aborts to safe P3. This prevents a stale callback from satisfying a later request.

I packaged a matching ARM64 kernel, module, CLI and initramfs through Docker, then booted the integration suite in disposable QEMU. The same controller also runs in a native pthread harness for fast model tests and sanitizer checks.
result: Validated all 16 state pairs, 10,000 randomized transitions and 50,000 adversarial register writes/ticks, alongside native address and undefined-behavior sanitizer checks.
The Linux guest completed 400 concurrent sysfs requests, fault-recovery checks, active-client removal and 10 module reload cycles. The tested kernel was Linux 6.1.190 ARM64.

Measured 200 alternating P0/P3 requests per backend: native-emulator p95 was 3.898 ms and QEMU sysfs p95 was 25.218 ms. These characterize the software request paths and scheduling, not physical GPU transitions.
takeaway: One owner per transition and an explicit recovery path keep concurrency manageable. The shared controller model makes the same state transitions testable in a fast native harness and a Linux guest.
technical: The shared model makes each voltage/frequency step inspectable. CURRENT stays at the last committed P-state until completion, while instantaneous voltage and frequency expose the intermediate transition.

The worker invokes the common interrupt handler in software. The QEMU guest validates Linux synchronization and lifecycle behavior; physical interrupt delivery and MMIO bus ordering require a separate hardware or virtual-device backend.
The controller uses invented electrical values and explicit thermal injection. It demonstrates power-management mechanisms without claiming to control an NVIDIA GPU or measure real GPU power.
CI runs native tests, sanitizers and Linux module compilation. The QEMU end-to-end suite is separately reproducible, with saved console evidence and a required pass marker.

implementation.use: Model register semantics, safe voltage/clock sequencing and deterministic fault injection.
Serialize callers, protect register state, wait for completion and drain work during recovery and removal.
Build a disposable ARM64 guest and validate concurrency, faults, teardown and memory safety.

title: Linux TPM Attestation & Device Integrity Monitor
headline: Trust the evidence. Catch the drift.
summary: Fresh TPM evidence, replay rejection and observable integrity checks. A Python verifier and Linux agent passed 22 tests, including eight-way concurrent replay.
label: passed with swtpm integration
problem: Device integrity needs fresh evidence and an operational response. I built an enrollment-to-monitoring workflow that verifies signed measurements, rejects reused reports and exposes the reason for each verdict.
approach: I built a Python Linux agent around tpm2-tools and swtpm. An administrator approves an attestation key and a baseline; the agent then requests a fresh verifier challenge and collects PCR measurements and configuration-file hashes.

The TPM quote binds its measurements to the challenge and report. My FastAPI verifier checks freshness, the enrolled signing key, RSA signature, PCR selection and approved baseline before storing a verdict in SQLite. Single-use challenges make a previously valid quote unusable as a new report.

I added Prometheus metrics and a Grafana dashboard so integrity failures are visible beyond an API response. Docker Compose runs the verifier and monitoring services, while isolated test state keeps the attack scenarios reproducible.

I tested the negative paths deliberately: reused challenges, modified signatures, changed configuration, PCR16 extension, expired nonces, wrong keys and device revocation. The demo also restores configuration to show the difference between a persistent problem and a successful recovery.
result: Passed all 22 automated tests with no skips in the swtpm-enabled Linux container; GitHub Actions also passed the container build and test suite.
Cross-checked a TPM-generated quote with both my Python verifier and tpm2_checkquote. Tests include eight-way concurrent replay and malformed, truncated and trailing evidence.

The live demo produced two verified events, one replay rejection, one signature rejection, one configuration rejection and four PCR-drift rejections. Prometheus scraped the verdicts, and Grafana exposed the provisioned three-panel dashboard.
takeaway: Freshness, identity and measurement integrity are separate checks. Making each visible gives an operator a usable security workflow, from enrollment through recovery.
technical: Replay handling needs to remain correct when requests arrive together, not just sequentially. Atomic challenge consumption and persistent verifier state are tested under concurrent reuse and restart scenarios.

Configuration hashes are agent-reported data, even when the quote binds them. I distinguish that binding from independently measured boot evidence: the lab does not validate EK certificates or replay measured-boot event logs.
The verifier checks selected PCRs against an approved baseline. A matching quote supports a specific integrity claim about those measurements; it does not prove that every part of a machine is safe.

The repository includes a protocol walkthrough, threat model, physical-hardware setup guide and reproducible attack-and-recovery demo. Services bind to localhost by default; remote operation requires TLS and controlled provisioning.

This completed lab uses swtpm in Linux containers. Physical-TPM validation and the host measured-boot chain are separate next steps; enrollment requires operator approval of the attestation key and baseline.

implementation.use: Generate signed PCR quotes in swtpm and independently cross-check them with tpm2_checkquote.
Enroll approved keys, issue single-use challenges, verify evidence and persist device verdicts.
Run a reproducible lab and expose integrity verdicts, rejection reasons and report freshness.

title: Gemma anomaly review
headline: Three signals. One story to review.
summary: Three panel agents, one shared Gemma adapter, one incident to review. I built the fine-tuning, serving and traceability path for a microgrid anomaly prototype.
label: one shared anomaly adapter
problem: Individual electrical panels can produce related anomaly signals. The aim was to turn those signals into one reviewable incident without changing the existing appliance-inference service.
approach: I built three logical panel agents around one Gemma adapter, conditioned on panel identity, and coordinated their outputs into a shared incident.
I fine-tuned with QLoRA, Hugging Face PEFT and TRL on Lambda GPUs, served with vLLM, and connected Respan traces to a Google Sheets review workflow through Nango.
I generated rule-derived training labels by replaying the existing anomaly engine over archived readings.
result: Delivered a hackathon prototype combining shared-adapter serving, execution traces and a human review path.
Integrated anomaly assistance alongside the existing BiLSTM / ONNX inference service.
note: Completed refers to the prototype. Independent anomaly-detection accuracy and production alert outcomes are not established.
technical: Panel identity conditions a shared adapter rather than requiring three separately fine-tuned models. The incident coordinator combines those panel-level outputs into one reviewable event.
QLoRA reduces the fine-tuning memory requirement; vLLM handles serving. Respan traces and the Sheets review workflow expose model behavior, but do not by themselves establish anomaly accuracy.
Training labels came from rule-engine replay because the source anomaly table contained only two verification rows. The prototype does not establish independently measured anomaly accuracy.

implementation.use: Fine-tune one shared adapter conditioned on panel identity.
Serve the model for the three panel agents.
Trace outputs and connect incidents to a Sheets review workflow.

takeaway: One shared adapter keeps the model layer compact; panel identity preserves context. The incident coordinator turns separate signals into one reviewable output.

title: ESP32 Microgrid Meter
headline: Small processor. Measured performance.
summary: ESP-IDF C firmware sustained 3,846 samples/s per channel in a two-second benchmark, with 17.5× faster fixed-point processing. Appliance sensing and Pi telemetry are designed next steps.
label: per channel · two-second ADC benchmark
problem: Appliance-level measurements can strengthen Microgrid Manager’s panel-level estimates. I first benchmarked acquisition and arithmetic on the ESP32-C3, then specified the isolated sensing and telemetry design.
approach: Wrote ESP-IDF C benchmarks for two-channel continuous ADC acquisition, blocking reads, LEDC loopback timing and fixed-point arithmetic.
Designed an isolated 9 V AC transformer front end with a biased divider. The power-meter proposal adds an SCT-013-030 current clamp.
Specified one JSON update per second over Wi-Fi to a Raspberry Pi, then Kafka forwarding using the eGauge field layout. MQTT publication to Home Assistant is a proposed extension.
result: Sustained 3,846 samples/s per channel with no dropped or foreign samples during a two-second continuous-ADC run.
Measured 16,666.40 µs mean period and 0.49 µs standard deviation across 1,289 periods of a 60 Hz LEDC loopback signal, with Wi-Fi off.
Fixed-point multiply-accumulate took 38.4 cycles/sample versus 673.1 for software float—a 17.5× improvement. A blocking ADC read took 48.6 µs.
takeaway: Continuous acquisition and fixed-point arithmetic give this small processor a practical processing budget. The next build stages are the isolated front end, reference-meter calibration and Pi telemetry.
technical: The board is an ESP32-C3-DevKit-RUST with RUST-2 I2C wiring; firmware is flashed from the Pi over USB. C is the current implementation language; a Rust sampling-loop port is a stretch goal.

Targets, not results: real power within 3% of a reference meter above 100 W; frequency agreement within 1 mHz; voltage sag/swell detection within one cycle. Proposed validation loads are a kettle and a fan or laptop charger, using a Kill A Watt P4400 reference.
Home Assistant was absent from the original proposals. Adding MQTT to the custom ESP-IDF firmware is the proposed integration path. No Pi deployment or newer hardware work has been verified.

Completed work consists of two proposals and benchmark firmware. The voltage transformer and current clamp have not been bought or wired; appliance voltage, power accuracy and end-to-end telemetry latency have not been measured.

implementation.use: Benchmark two-channel acquisition and compare continuous sampling with blocking reads.
Measure loopback timing and arithmetic cost on a processor without an FPU.
Forward appliance readings to Microgrid Manager and optionally Home Assistant.

title: GPT-2 on the CPU
headline: Make every cache line count.
summary: Cut the hot kernel’s L1 data-cache miss rate from 9.17% to 2–3% using Linux perf, cache tiling and AVX2 vectorization in GPT-2 matrix multiplication.
label: reported L1 cache-miss rate
problem: Matrix multiplication dominated the CPU training loop. I used hardware counters to choose where to optimize, then improved the memory access and arithmetic inside those kernels.
approach: Linux perf attributed 33.09% of sampled cycles to backward matrix multiplication and 23.88% to forward multiplication, setting the optimization priorities.
I tiled the computation for data reuse and used AVX2 fused multiply-add instructions to process eight floats at a time within the existing build constraints.
Related experiments examined thread scaling, page sizes and NUMA locality to connect code changes with processor behavior.
result: Reduced the hot kernel’s L1 data-cache miss rate from 9.17% to approximately 2–3% in follow-up profiling.
Implemented cache tiling and vectorized matrix arithmetic, using hardware counters to evaluate the changes.
note: This is a kernel cache-behavior result. The archived material does not establish a reproducible end-to-end training speedup.
technical: The optimization targets memory reuse inside matrix multiplication. Tiling changes the working set; AVX2 changes the arithmetic issued per instruction. These mechanisms need separate measurements because lower cache-miss rates alone do not establish total speedup.

Compiler flags, matrix dimensions and thread settings need to stay fixed when comparing kernel changes. I used hardware counters to connect the observed cache-miss reduction to the memory-access changes.

My optimization work focuses on matmul_forward and matmul_backward and their pthread helpers. Integration had to stay within an existing notebook build, without adding compiler flags or external libraries.

implementation.use: Find the CPU kernels and cache misses that dominate execution.
Pack matrix tiles and vectorize multiply–accumulate work.
Split matrix work across CPU threads within the existing build.

takeaway: Profile the expensive work, improve locality, then vectorize. Separate measurements make it possible to connect an optimization to the behavior it actually changes.

title: Osmosis
headline: A world built from clock cycles.
summary: Eight moving molecules and a selective membrane at 640 × 480. I built the game in structural Verilog and verified two display frames with zero sync or RGB-blanking errors.
label: VGA display pipeline
problem: The challenge was to build a playable VGA game under strict structural-RTL constraints: continuous assignments and flip-flop primitives, with no procedural blocks in the hardware design.
approach: I separated pixel timing from frame-based movement and composed collision handling, membrane controls, randomized motion, a timer and game-state logic.
I used FDRE configuration-time initialization to establish molecule positions before the derived clock began, alongside synchronous runtime reset.
Behavioral simulation stubs, timing tests and bitmap rendering checked the control logic and visible output.
result: The provided display testbench completed two frames with zero sync errors and zero RGB-blanking errors.
Implemented eight moving molecules, color-selective membrane control and randomized positions, speeds and directions.
note: The animated card is a visual interpretation of the game, not a recording of the FPGA output.
technical: Pixel counters produce display coordinates and blanking signals; frame pulses advance object motion. Separating these time scales keeps collision and game-state updates independent of pixel traversal.

Configuration-time FDRE INIT values solve a different problem from synchronous runtime reset. The start-position failure required checking the clock-start sequence and rendered pixels, not just the state-machine transitions.

implementation.use: Compose game state and movement from structural logic.
Drive pixel coordinates, blanking and color output.
Check display timing and visible object positions.

takeaway: Pixel timing and game state run at different rates. Clear boundaries between them let small synchronous components form a responsive, visible system.

title: HTTP / HTTPS proxy
headline: The fastest repeat request is already here.
summary: 50% lower cached-response time in my benchmark. A concurrent C proxy combines bounded FIFO / LRU caching with HTTPS CONNECT tunneling.
label: lower cached response time
problem: Repeated requests should reuse completed work. I built a concurrent proxy that balances faster cached responses with bounded storage, correct response framing and synchronized access.
approach: I implemented FIFO and LRU eviction with a shared cache, keyed by the requested resource. Cache updates are synchronized, and incomplete or oversized responses are excluded.
The documented detached-thread variant uses POSIX threads for clients and CONNECT tunneling for HTTPS, relaying encrypted bytes without terminating the client’s TLS session.
A separate thread-pool variant explored bounded work queues and clean shutdown. I keep those designs distinct when discussing their concurrency behavior.
result: Reduced cached response time by 50% in my cached-response benchmark.
Built HTTP response caching with a 1 MB per-response bound and HTTPS CONNECT forwarding.
I exercised argument validation, cache-policy sequences, response-body checks, sanitizer runs and concurrent-request exercises.
note: The 50% result applies to the cached-response benchmark reported on my resume; it is not a universal speedup across uncached requests or HTTPS tunnels.
technical: A cache entry is reusable only when the full HTTP response is available and within the size bound. A mutex protects shared cache mutation; the linked-list order implements FIFO insertion order or LRU recency.
HTTPS CONNECT is a bidirectional byte tunnel in the documented variant. TLS remains between client and origin, so the proxy cannot treat the encrypted payload as an ordinary cacheable HTTP response.

implementation.use: Parse HTTP requests and relay client/origin traffic.
Protect shared entries and manage eviction order.
Forward encrypted traffic as a bidirectional byte tunnel.

takeaway: The cache improves latency when a complete response can be safely reused. Bounded entries and explicit synchronization keep the performance benefit tied to correct network behavior.

title: Tesphase
headline: Listen first. Build what matters.
summary: 30+ customer interviews became a React Native solar app with authentication, real-time sync and push notifications. I led the roadmap and architecture; Tesphase won SC Launchpad 2025.
label: customer-discovery interviews
problem: Solar homeowners needed an approachable way to coordinate their energy use. At Tesphase, my role as CTO was to connect customer needs with a practical product roadmap and working application.
approach: I translated more than 30 NSF I-Corps customer interviews into product priorities and owned the engineering roadmap.
I led a React Native mobile architecture with Supabase authentication and real-time data, plus Node.js backend workflows.
result: Delivered authentication, real-time database synchronization and push notifications.
Won SC Launchpad 2025. I served as CTO from April through September 2025.
note: Proposed bill savings in the early lean canvas were product hypotheses, not measured customer outcomes.
technical: Authentication establishes the user identity used by application data. Real-time synchronization and push notifications serve different paths: updating shared state in the app versus drawing attention to an event. Product interviews informed which workflows received engineering effort first.
Early energy-savings estimates were product hypotheses for customer validation, not measured savings.

implementation.use: Build the mobile interface around customer priorities.
Support authentication and synchronized application data.
Connect backend workflows to the product roadmap.

takeaway: Customer discovery gave the roadmap its order. Architecture and delivery turned those priorities into working product features.

title: Slug Board
headline: Campus events. Connected.
summary: Event creation, RSVPs, upvotes and comments for campus life. I owned the SQL schema and event workflows and coordinated a React / Supabase migration as Scrum Master.
label: events, RSVPs and comments
problem: Campus activities are easy to miss when information stays inside separate college communities. Our team built Slug Board to bring event discovery and participation together.
approach: I owned event CRUD, the SQL schema and backend interaction logic for RSVPs, upvotes and comments.
I consolidated authentication, event and profile lookups in application code around a shared Profiles model during the move to React and Supabase.
As Sprint 2 Scrum Master, I helped coordinate the stack migration alongside feature delivery.
result: Implemented event CRUD, SQL schema and updates, and event-card interaction logic for RSVPs, upvotes and comments.
Coordinated the React / Supabase stack migration as Sprint 2 Scrum Master.
note: The archived reflection reports a 37.5% team completion rate for the MVP stage. It documents the learning and integration failures rather than a successful product launch.
technical: The retrospective identifies the critical integration boundary: event-card interactions depended on authentication, API behavior and database queries that were not consistently verified together.

The corrective approach is to validate endpoints and database contracts before wiring the interface, integrate across user stories earlier, and keep local branches synchronized. These are lessons from the retrospective, not claims of a subsequently rebuilt MVP.
The coursework finished with 37.5% of the planned MVP. Backend integration remained incomplete; the event-workflow contribution does not represent a completed production application.

implementation.use: Build event cards and participation interactions.
Model profiles, events, RSVPs, votes and comments.
Coordinate the stack migration and feature work across the team.

takeaway: Event discovery depends on a complete path through identity, APIs and database state. Shared interface contracts and early integration are the central engineering lessons from this team project.

title: HTTP server on FPGA
headline: From sockets to silicon.
summary: A C server becomes the behavioral reference for an FPGA design. This ongoing port explores request parsing, buffering and board bring-up.
label: software as a behavioral reference
problem: This project connects two areas of my work: network programming in C and synchronous digital design.
approach: I use the software server as a reference while exploring how request handling, buffering and board bring-up translate into FPGA hardware.
The work considers the Spartan-3E, Basys3 and Alchitry hardware mentioned in my project record.
result: The current outcome is a porting and bring-up effort.
The next milestone is an end-to-end HTTP request served on hardware.
note: A working hardware server and hardware performance figures are not yet established.
technical: The software server provides reference behavior for request parsing and responses. Buffering, state sequencing and the hardware network interface remain design constraints to resolve before an end-to-end board demonstration.

implementation.use: Use software request behavior as the porting reference.
Explore buffering and synchronous request-handling logic.
Work toward an end-to-end hardware request; this milestone remains open.

takeaway: The software reference defines the behavior; the hardware port makes buffering, state sequencing and interfaces explicit. The next milestone is a complete request served on the FPGA.

title: Two-player Quick Add
headline: Two players. One fair game.
summary: A nine-state controller gives two players one fair response window. Synchronized inputs, score logic and game-over handling passed both recorded testbenches.
label: round and score controller
problem: Expanding a single-player game requires a shared response window, independent player state and correct handling of simultaneous inputs.
approach: I synchronized and latched button inputs so both players could answer inside the same round window.
I coordinated score updates and game-over transitions across clock boundaries, including lockout at zero points.
result: Both recorded testbenches passed after the fix, including ties, simultaneous wrong answers, no-response rounds and game-over lockout.
note: The project demonstrates structural control logic and focused verification.
technical: Two-flop synchronizers bring button signals into the clock domain; round latches retain each player’s response. The one-hot FSM resolves the shared window into scoring and the next round.

The score register and game controller observe values on clock boundaries. Explicit game-over transitions handle the updated score on the following cycle rather than assuming it is immediately visible.

implementation.use: Implement round control and registered score state.
Capture each player’s answer within a shared response window.
Check ties, missed answers and game-over transitions.

takeaway: A shared response window makes fairness an explicit hardware rule. Tests for ties, simultaneous inputs and no response exercise that rule at its boundaries.

title: Quick Decode & counter lab
headline: Small circuits. A larger foundation.
summary: From a 16-bit counter to a reaction game: structural Verilog, seven-segment output and one-hot control formed the foundation for my later VGA work.
label: loadable up/down counter
problem: Digital logic coursework moved from a stateful counter and display to reaction games with explicit sequencing.
approach: I built a 16-bit loadable up/down counter with seven-segment display output.
Quick Decode and Quick Add extended that foundation with one-hot state machines and LFSR-based logic under structural design constraints.

Earlier labs built an 8-bit ripple-carry adder/subtractor, two’s-complement sign changer, multiplexers and hexadecimal seven-segment decoding. Those components supplied the arithmetic and display foundation for the counter and games.
result: Completed the counter and reaction-game labs, building the synchronous design foundation used later in the Osmosis VGA game.
note: Coursework progression; no hardware performance benchmark is claimed.
technical: The counter lab exercises registered state, direction and load control. The reaction games add state sequencing and pseudo-random behavior; Osmosis extends the progression into display timing and moving objects.

implementation.use: Build loadable counters, arithmetic logic and registered state.
Display counter values and game output.
Add pseudo-random behavior and reaction-game sequencing.

takeaway: Counters, arithmetic and display logic form a reusable digital-design foundation. These labs carried directly into the timing and state machines of Osmosis.

title: Spiking neural networks
headline: Learning, one spike at a time.
summary: Spike encoding, neuron dynamics and training experiments with UCSC’s Neuromorphic Computing Group. Moving runs to Colab Pro cut reported epoch time from about seven minutes to under two.
label: encoding and training stability
problem: In UCSC’s Neuromorphic Computing Group, I study how spike encoding, neuron dynamics and normalization shape learning over time.
approach: On MNIST and CIFAR-10, I compared rate, Poisson and latency encodings, investigated threshold-dependent batch normalization and tuned membrane decay, firing thresholds and timesteps.
Layer activity, membrane behavior and loss traces helped separate dead neurons from optimizer and normalization failures.
A separate UCF101 prototype combined frozen ResNet18 features with a small spiking classifier. It remains a demonstration with a split-validation concern.
result: Built training pipelines and diagnostic traces across multiple spiking-network configurations.
Moving experiments to Colab Pro reduced reported epoch time from about seven minutes to under two.
note: No validated accuracy or energy-efficiency advantage over a conventional CNN is claimed.
technical: Spike encoding maps image intensity into temporal events. LIF neurons integrate current with membrane decay and emit spikes at a threshold; surrogate gradients approximate the non-differentiable threshold during training.

Spike-health traces, loss behavior and optimizer updates must be checked together. Active neurons alone did not guarantee learning, while normalization changes could leave initialized currents too weak to cross threshold.

implementation.use: Train spiking models and inspect membrane and firing behavior.
Compare rate, Poisson and latency encoding experiments.
Run training and examine loss and spike-health traces.

takeaway: Encoding, membrane dynamics and normalization shape the signal together. Inspecting spike activity alongside the loss makes that interaction visible.

title: ESP32 Weather Station in Rust
headline: Local readings. One connected Pi.
summary: An ESP32-C3 client in Rust connects onboard readings and outdoor weather to a Raspberry Pi HTTP service. Configuration, acquisition and reporting share an explicit device/server contract.
label: device-to-server workflow
problem: A small connected device needs to obtain configuration, gather sensor data and report readings to a service reliably.
approach: The ESP32-C3 fetches the server’s location, queries an outdoor-weather service and reads its onboard sensor.
The Raspberry Pi serves location data and accepts posted readings, separating device acquisition from server-side logging.
result: Implemented the device/server coursework workflow for configuration, acquisition and posted readings; embedded coursework is ongoing.
note: The onboard sensor reading should not be presented as a calibrated ambient-temperature measurement.
technical: The device obtains location from GET /location and posts its readings to the Raspberry Pi service. Separating configuration, acquisition and reporting makes the device/server protocol explicit.

implementation.use: Implement the ESP32-C3 acquisition and reporting client.
Fetch location, query outdoor weather and post readings.
Provide location configuration and accept device data.

takeaway: A clear device/server contract separates configuration from acquisition and reporting. That makes the firmware and Pi service easier to develop independently.

title: Battle Boats
headline: Your move. Powered by interrupts.
summary: Event-driven C on a PIC32MX: timer interrupts, UART messaging and OLED output bring Battleship-style state machines onto physical hardware.
label: event-driven embedded control
problem: A microcontroller game needs to respond to hardware events while keeping game state consistent.
approach: I organized Battleship-style gameplay as state machines and used timers, hardware interrupts and low-level peripheral drivers to connect software behavior to the board.
My implementation connects an Agent state machine to message parsing, negotiation, field state and OLED rendering. UART and circular-buffer modules carry the board-to-board message path.
result: Implemented Battleship-style gameplay on a PIC32MX in C, connecting state machines, UART messages, timer interrupts and OLED rendering.
note: No measured latency or performance benchmark is claimed.
technical: Timers and hardware interrupts supply events to the game state machines. Peripheral access and application state need clear boundaries so a hardware event produces one consistent state transition.

Separating negotiation, field updates and message events makes turn-taking explicit. The agent owns the transition between negotiation, attack, wait and end-game behavior while the display reflects that state.

implementation.use: Organize game behavior into an agent state machine.
Carry messages between boards.
Connect hardware events to gameplay and display state.

takeaway: The agent owns game state; peripheral drivers deliver events. That division keeps turn-taking and hardware behavior understandable as the system grows.

title: Concurrent HTTP file server
headline: Many requests. Consistent files.
summary: A multithreaded C file server coordinates GET / PUT requests, worker dispatch, resource locks and audit logging under concurrent access.
label: parsing, files and concurrency
problem: Concurrent clients can read and overwrite the same file. A server needs to parse partial network input correctly and coordinate file access so its responses and audit log tell a consistent story.
approach: I extended a single-connection GET / PUT server into a concurrent design, covering request validation, content lengths, response codes and socket/file cleanup.
I implemented worker dispatch, per-resource reader–writer locking and serialized audit logging, with explicit handling for partial network reads.
result: Implemented the HTTP file-server coursework and documented the progression from protocol parsing to concurrent request handling.
The software work also provides the behavioral starting point for my separate FPGA HTTP experiment.
note: Completed describes the coursework implementation. The archive includes unresolved build and parsing iterations; it does not establish a production deployment or a throughput benchmark.
technical: A successful socket read can return only part of a request. The parser must preserve bytes already received after the header terminator and account for the remaining body before completing a PUT.
File locking and audit ordering are separate correctness concerns. Protecting file contents does not automatically make the log reflect the same operation order.

implementation.use: Handle partial requests, GET / PUT operations and responses.
Dispatch clients and coordinate shared-file access.
Work through build failures and protocol behavior.

takeaway: Correct concurrency crosses the whole request path: parsing, file access, response construction and audit order. Resource ownership ties those pieces together.

title: Thread-safe queue & reader–writer locks
headline: Shared work. Ordered access.
summary: One bounded work queue and three reader–writer admission policies. Built in C with pthreads, mutexes and condition variables.
label: reader, writer and bounded-reader modes
problem: Producers and consumers need to exchange work without racing, while shared resources need a clear rule for admitting readers and writers.
approach: I implemented a circular queue with head, tail and occupancy state guarded by a mutex. Separate condition variables represent available items and available capacity.
I implemented reader-preference, writer-preference and bounded-reader lock modes, tracking active and waiting participants to make admission policy explicit.
result: Built reusable queue and lock modules for the concurrent-systems coursework.
Made the tradeoff between throughput and waiting behavior a configurable part of the lock design.
note: The archive contains implementation and debugging work; it does not provide a verified starvation-freedom or stress-test result.
technical: Waiters recheck their predicates while holding the mutex after waking. A signal announces that state may have changed; it does not reserve an item or grant a lock.
An N-way policy limits reader admission when a writer is waiting. Correctness depends on maintaining the counters and wake-up conditions together.

implementation.use: Track head, tail and occupancy in a bounded queue.
Protect state and coordinate waiting producers and consumers.
Implement reader, writer and bounded-reader admission policies.

takeaway: Admission policy changes who makes progress under contention. Exposing three policies makes that tradeoff part of the lock’s interface.

title: Command-driven file I/O
headline: Bytes in. Files out.
summary: A C command-line utility turns get / set requests into explicit Unix file operations, with byte-counted input and resource cleanup.
label: command protocol over standard input
problem: A small file utility still has to distinguish command metadata from payload bytes, handle failed system calls and avoid assuming that one read or write transfers everything.
approach: I worked on a memory.c utility that reads get and set commands from standard input and maps them to file reads or replacements.
The implementation and review covered command parsing, declared payload length, file-opening flags, error messages and releasing allocated buffers and descriptors.
result: Built the file-I/O coursework foundation used later in HTTP request handling.
The project made byte counts, input boundaries and cleanup explicit parts of the interface.
note: Coursework implementation; the archived iterations do not establish a complete binary-data or large-file correctness suite.
technical: Text tokenization is appropriate for command fields, but payloads require byte-counted handling. The review exposed why treating the whole input as a null-terminated string is fragile.

implementation.use: Map get / set commands to file-descriptor operations.
Separate command fields from declared payload bytes.
Build and debug the command-line utility.

takeaway: Byte counts and file descriptors make the protocol concrete. Explicit input boundaries and cleanup keep command parsing aligned with the filesystem operations it requests.

title: Pac-Man search agents
headline: Look ahead. Choose better.
summary: Reflex, minimax and alpha–beta agents turn a game tree into the next move. Python coursework connects heuristic evaluation with adversarial search.
label: state evaluation and action selection
problem: Greedy movement can trap an agent near food or a ghost. Planning requires a consistent model of turns, terminal states and the consequences of an action.
approach: I worked on reflex evaluation and adversarial search agents, using food distance, ghost proximity and scared timers to score successor states.
I debugged state-versus-position mistakes, repeated movement and depth handling, then ran repeated games without graphics to inspect outcomes across layouts.
result: Produced runnable agents and recorded wins, losses and scores during coursework experiments.
The experiments exposed how strongly performance depends on the layout, evaluator and depth setting.
note: The recorded runs use different configurations. I do not present a single selected win rate as a general benchmark.
technical: Minimax assumes an adversarial opponent; expectimax models chance. Alpha–beta pruning reduces unnecessary search while preserving the minimax decision for the same tree and evaluator.

implementation.use: Generate successor states and run repeated games.
Choose moves under adversarial assumptions and prune search.
Explore chance-based opponents and score food/ghost tradeoffs.

takeaway: The evaluation function gives the search its priorities; depth determines how far it can test them. Keeping those decisions separate makes agent behavior easier to inspect.

title: Gridworld & Pac-Man reinforcement learning
headline: Learn by playing.
summary: Value iteration and Q-learning agents make the exploration–exploitation tradeoff visible in Gridworld and Pac-Man.
label: learning action values from rewards
problem: A useful action may require exploring a risky route before its reward is known. The challenge is to learn from experience while keeping training behavior separate from evaluation.
approach: I implemented action-value updates and epsilon-greedy selection, working through unseen state-action values, terminal states and ties between legal actions.
I used Gridworld and Pac-Man exercises to examine how learning rate, discounting and exploration affect the policy, including the BridgeGrid scenario and feature-based value approximation.
result: Built and debugged the learning-agent coursework and compared sampled learning with model-based value iteration.
The work made exploration settings and training versus test episodes explicit experimental choices.
note: No transferable win-rate or sample-efficiency improvement is claimed from the archived coursework.
technical: The Q update moves the current estimate toward reward plus the discounted best next-state value. A terminal transition has no future action value; handling that case prevents invalid action lookups.

implementation.use: Run Gridworld and Pac-Man learning exercises.
Update action values from observed transitions and rewards.
Compare exploration-based learning with model-based planning.

takeaway: Exploration gathers experience; evaluation measures the resulting policy. Separate training and test episodes make learning-rate and discount choices comparable.

title: Capture-the-flag agents
headline: Attack. Defend. Adapt.
summary: Two agents balance collecting food with protecting territory. A Python policy combines role switching, maze distances and spatial heuristics.
label: context-dependent agent behavior
problem: Two agents must collect food, protect home territory and avoid interfering with each other. A fixed offensive or defensive role cannot respond to every board state.
approach: I developed weighted features for food, capsules, visible opponents, teammate distance and returning home, with attack/defense switching as the board changes.
I tuned stop/reverse penalties, corridor handling and trap-avoidance behavior using maze-distance features.
result: Implemented a cooperative team policy and documented its representation, decision rules and evaluation limits.
note: The archive supports implementation and report work, but does not establish a tournament placement or a controlled improvement over a baseline.
technical: Maze distance captures walls that Manhattan distance ignores. Feature weights still need care: rewarding distance from a teammate or opponent too strongly can overpower the goal of making progress.

implementation.use: Implement a cooperative capture-the-flag policy.
Measure routes around walls to food, allies and threats.
Switch between attack and defense and penalize traps or reversal.

takeaway: A useful team policy makes competing goals explicit: collect rewards, protect territory and coordinate movement.

title: AVL word-range index
headline: Count the range. Skip the scan.
summary: An augmented AVL tree uses subtree sizes to answer word-range queries through rank traversal, keeping balance and query metadata together.
label: subtree sizes alongside balance metadata
problem: A word index needs to accept insertions while answering how many entries lie between two keys. An unbalanced tree or a full traversal makes those queries unnecessarily expensive.
approach: I implemented an AVL tree that stores height and subtree size, with rotations maintaining both balance and rank-query metadata.
I checked insertion sequences, rotation order and lexicographic comparisons against expected range counts.
result: Built the indexed-query coursework around two rank traversals per range count, with explicit checks of subtree-size invariants.
note: Logarithmic query complexity is a property of the correctly maintained AVL design, not a measured speedup. The archive includes debugging cases without a final comprehensive pass report.
technical: For inclusive bounds, count(keys ≤ upper) − count(keys < lower) handles the boundary correctly. Heights and sizes must be recomputed after rotations in child-before-parent order.

implementation.use: Maintain a balanced index as words are inserted.
Compute inclusive range counts from two rank traversals.
Trace incorrect counts through height, size and comparison updates.

takeaway: Subtree sizes turn a balanced tree into a rank index. Maintaining them through rotations is what makes range queries efficient and reliable.

title: Six Degrees: actor connection finder
headline: Two actors. The shortest connection.
summary: Find a shortest actor connection—and the films behind every step. A C++ graph pairs breadth-first search with traceable path reconstruction.
label: shortest paths with movie provenance
problem: A connection finder needs to return more than a distance: the user should see which shared films connect the actors.
approach: I parsed cast lists, mapped actor and movie names to integer IDs and stored movie IDs with actor-to-actor edges.
Breadth-first search tracks visited actors and records both the previous actor and the film used to reach each node. I reconstruct the path from that parent map.
result: Built a file-driven C++ program that reconstructs a shortest connection as an actor-and-film chain.
Handled parsing, disconnected inputs and predecessor reconstruction as part of the query interface.
note: The archived implementation uses pairwise cast connections; a movie with a large cast can create many edges. No large-dataset performance claim is made.
technical: BFS finds a shortest path by edge count in an unweighted graph. Keeping movie identity on the predecessor edge preserves an explanation of why each connection exists.

implementation.use: Map actor and movie names to compact IDs.
Find the fewest actor-to-actor connections.
Recover both the actors and films explaining the path.

takeaway: A shortest path becomes useful when it explains each connection. Recording film provenance during traversal preserves that explanation at the output.

title: Data structures & constraint-solving lab
headline: Build the structures. Understand the work.
summary: C and C++ implementations spanning linked lists, graph traversal, word indexes and constraint search. Each makes memory ownership and algorithm state explicit.
label: from memory ownership to search
problem: High-level containers hide the state changes that make an algorithm work. These exercises made memory ownership, traversal state and constraints explicit.
approach: I built linked-list and graph ADTs, indirect lexicographic sorting, a deck-shuffle client and a Shakespeare word-frequency index grouped by word length.

I worked on N-Queens with preset placements and an explicit search stack, alongside stack-based anagram generation and smaller simulation exercises. Debugging focused on preserving fixed constraints while undoing only speculative choices.
result: Built command-line coursework programs with file-based inputs and outputs across data structures and constraint search.
Corrected N-Queens backtracking to preserve valid preset placements.
note: These are educational implementations, grouped here rather than presented as separate production products.
technical: An explicit stack must retain enough state to resume a search after backtracking. A linked-list cursor must distinguish being off-list from pointing at a valid node; that invariant affects insertion and deletion alike.

implementation.use: Build ADTs, word indexes and indirect sorting clients.
Represent connections and explore reachable states.
Resume constraint search while preserving fixed N-Queens placements.

takeaway: Explicit state makes algorithms debuggable. Small counterexamples expose ownership, traversal and backtracking errors before they disappear inside a larger input.

title: Virtual network topology lab
headline: A network. Before the hardware.
summary: A repeatable Python / Mininet topology connects hosts through two switches and traffic-controlled links for hands-on network experiments.
label: repeatable network setup
problem: A network diagram does not show whether host interfaces, links and addressing behave as intended. Emulation makes those relationships inspectable.
approach: I worked through a Python topology representing user devices and home equipment connected through two switches.
I configured host/link definitions and used the Mininet environment to inspect interface state and distinguish host commands from the surrounding Linux shell.
result: Developed a Python / Mininet lab topology with two switches, emulated hosts and traffic-controlled links.
Used the topology to inspect interface state and distinguish host commands from commands inside node namespaces.
note: This is a topology and configuration exercise; the export does not establish a verified routing policy or measured throughput.
technical: Adding a link does not by itself solve addressing or routing. Host namespaces and switch connectivity need to be checked separately when diagnosing reachability.

implementation.use: Define virtual hosts, switches and links.
Configure link behavior for the topology exercise.
Inspect interfaces and distinguish host commands from the outer shell.

takeaway: A repeatable virtual topology brings network boundaries into view before a physical bench is required.

title: Saaf / Saaf Safai
headline: Shared chores. A simpler start.
summary: Welcome screens and authentication prototypes for shared chores. React Native and Next.js explorations establish the entry point for a future reminder workflow.
label: mobile and web explorations
problem: Chore coordination starts with a low-friction entry into the application. Before building reminder logic, the interface and development environment need a reliable foundation.
approach: I prototyped the React Native welcome screen and configured its simulator and Metro workflow.
A separate Next.js / Supabase exploration established the web login path.
result: Established the app concept, welcome-screen work and authentication scaffold.
The next meaningful milestone is an integrated chore workflow with persistence and reminders.
note: The mobile and web experiments are distinct prototypes. Completed reminder scheduling, production authentication and an app release are not established.
technical: I worked through obsolete CLI paths, missing Metro configuration and package setup before tackling feature integration. A reliable development toolchain is the first dependency of the chore workflow.

implementation.use: Explore the mobile welcome screen and simulator setup.
Prototype a separate web login path.
Work through dependency and project-configuration failures.

takeaway: The current prototypes establish entry and authentication. The next product milestone connects them to persisted chores and reminders.

title: StanChat
headline: Write. Sync. Stay connected.
summary: Send a message, see it arrive, scroll back through the conversation. A local Flutter / Firebase prototype connects the complete message path.
label: locally confirmed message flow
problem: A short MVP timeline calls for one useful vertical slice: write a message, see it appear and keep conversation history available.
approach: I moved toward Flutter for a shared cross-platform interface and Firebase for managed storage. The chat screen listens to Firestore message updates and writes text with timestamps.
I worked through FlutterFire setup, dependency conflicts and Android emulator configuration, prioritizing the message path before additional account features.
result: Built a local message flow: send a message, see it in the conversation, and scroll back through earlier messages.
Reached a working local chat prototype; broader release and account workflows were later milestones.
note: Completed refers to the local prototype. Public deployment, multi-device validation and production access-control readiness are not established.
technical: A stream-driven interface updates the conversation when stored messages change. Database permissions and identity become essential before expanding a local demonstration into a shared public service.

implementation.use: Build the message composer and scrollable conversation.
Write timestamped messages and listen for updates.
Configure the integration and reach a working local chat demo.

takeaway: One complete message path makes the architecture testable: compose, persist, receive and render. The local prototype establishes that path before broader account and release work.

title: iOS voice-recorder modernization
headline: Keep the recordings. Modernize the app.
summary: Swift / UIKit modernization of a legacy recording app targeting iOS 18, spanning audio controls, delegate callbacks and persisted recording metadata.
label: legacy UI and audio workflows
problem: An existing recording app combined audio, persistence, advertising and third-party UI components. Platform changes exposed compatibility and maintenance issues across those boundaries.
approach: I worked through AppDelegate, recording and table-cell code, tracing record/playback controls, delegate callbacks and stored recording metadata.
I requested a native replacement for a rating component that was failing on iOS 18 and reviewed supporting API and integration errors.
result: Produced modernization work across the legacy application’s UI and recording paths.
The focus was compatibility and maintainability of an existing codebase, with device validation still needed.
note: This is maintenance of an existing application, not a claim of creating the original app. The archive does not confirm an App Store release or complete iOS 18 validation.
technical: Audio-session state, playback controls and persisted file metadata need to stay consistent. A UI migration is incomplete until recording, interruption, playback and deletion behavior are checked on a device.

implementation.use: Modernize legacy screens and delegate interactions.
Review recording/playback behavior and stored metadata.
Replace an incompatible rating dependency as part of iOS 18 work.

takeaway: Modernization begins with the recording lifecycle: audio state, callbacks and file metadata must stay aligned as the interface changes. Device validation completes that work.

title: 8-bit TTL computer
headline: Eight bits. Every part accounted for.
summary: An 8-bit computer architecture and staged build proposal: ALU, registers, program counter, memory and control, planned as independently testable modules.
label: architecture and build plan
problem: Computer architecture can remain abstract when the datapath and control signals are hidden inside a processor. A discrete build makes those boundaries visible.
approach: I developed a proposal covering the ALU, register bank, program counter, instruction storage, shared bus and control sequence.
I organized the work into module-level checks, integration, simple instruction programs and documentation, with a component budget and a staged build schedule.
result: Produced the architecture, build sequence and funding proposal.
A functioning assembled computer remains a future hardware milestone.
note: The archive documents a proposal and research, not completed hardware, awarded funding or measured processor performance.
technical: The proposed integration checks include bus contention, clock distribution and control timing. Each datapath module needs independent verification before the fetch–decode–execute sequence can be validated.

implementation.use: Plan independently testable ALU and register modules.
Design the proposed instruction/control sequence.
Define integration checks; physical completion remains a future milestone.

takeaway: The proposal makes each datapath module independently testable, then stages integration around the fetch–decode–execute cycle.

title: Spotify playlist analyzer
headline: Start with a playlist. Ask a better question.
summary: A Python project proposal turning playlist data into an analysis workflow: API retrieval, structured features and a planned regression experiment.
label: project design and starter workflow
problem: A playlist is a useful starting point for learning how an API response becomes a structured dataset and an interpretable analysis.
approach: I scoped a playlist-analysis project and explored how to organize API retrieval, data preparation and a linear-regression experiment.
I worked on repository structure and documentation before committing to a finished interface or predictive claim.
result: Defined the analysis direction and starter project structure.
Data access, a reproducible dataset and evaluation remain prerequisites for a finished result.
note: This is an exploratory proposal. The archive does not establish current API access, a trained predictor or recommendation quality.
technical: The analysis needs a clearly defined target and held-out evaluation. Descriptive playlist statistics and a predictive regression model answer different questions.

implementation.use: Plan playlist retrieval and structured data preparation.
Scope descriptive analysis and a predictive experiment.
Organize starter documentation; evaluated modeling is still proposed.

takeaway: The analysis question defines the dataset and target. Reproducible retrieval and held-out evaluation are the next steps in the proposed workflow.

title: Market-data forecasting study
headline: A forecast starts with a fair test.
summary: A team research plan for the Jane Street forecasting problem, pairing an XGBoost baseline with feature selection and a possible LSTM comparison.
label: baseline and follow-up model plan
problem: Financial observations can shift over time and contain heavy noise. A forecasting project must define a credible evaluation before treating a fitted pattern as useful signal.
approach: I contributed to the project framing and presentation around a boosting baseline, feature selection and a possible LSTM follow-up.
The planned comparison separates tabular feature interactions from sequence effects and calls for evaluation on data outside the fitting period.
result: Developed the technical approach, project schedule and presentation materials.
The next evidence needed is a reproducible training run and out-of-period validation.
note: The export documents planning and presentation work. It does not substantiate a leaderboard score, successful backtest or trading return.
technical: Chronological validation matters because random splits can mix future information into training. A complex sequence model needs to justify its cost against the baseline on the same evaluation period.

implementation.use: Plan a baseline for interactions in noisy tabular features.
Propose a follow-up experiment for sequence effects.
Define out-of-period evaluation before claiming predictive value.

takeaway: Respecting time is the key evaluation decision. Later-period validation gives the baseline and a sequence model a common test.

title: Analog circuits & filter characterization
headline: From equations to waveforms.
summary: Circuit theory meets measured amplitude and phase. Lab reports cover DC equivalents, transients and filter frequency response.
label: transient and steady-state analysis
problem: A transfer function predicts behavior, but a bench circuit adds loading, component tolerance and measurement choices. The task was to connect observed voltage and phase to the model.
approach: I worked through KCL/KVL, superposition and Thévenin/Norton equivalents, then analyzed capacitor and inductor transients using the single-time-constant model.
For sinusoidal filters, I used the supplied measurement data to build gain and phase tables and Bode plots, relating time delay to phase and comparing low-pass and high-pass behavior.
result: Produced lab analyses and reports spanning DC equivalents, transient behavior and frequency response.
The work connected amplitude and timing observations to the equations used to design filters.
note: These are coursework measurements and analyses. No component-accuracy or instrumentation-performance improvement is claimed.
technical: Magnitude is expressed as 20 log10(Vout/Vin). Phase follows from the time shift at the measurement frequency; both the sign convention and the distinction between peak and peak-to-peak values matter.

implementation.use: Study equivalent circuits, transients and filters.
Relate observed amplitude and delay to circuit behavior.
Compare frequency-dependent gain and phase with the model.

takeaway: Transient and frequency measurements describe the same circuit from different angles. Comparing both connects component choices to the observed response.

title: Expression trees for generative art
headline: Small expressions. Generative art.
summary: A Haskell expression tree turns coordinates, arithmetic and trigonometry into composable image formulas with inspectable structure.
label: composition, traversal and depth
problem: A procedural image can be represented as an expression evaluated at coordinates. The representation needs to support composition while remaining easy to inspect and traverse.
approach: I worked with an Expr type containing coordinate variables, sine, cosine, averaging, multiplication and threshold branches.
I implemented recursive depth calculation and constructed a compound expression combining the two coordinates with trigonometric functions.
result: Built the expression representation and depth-traversal exercise.
The result makes a visual formula inspectable as a tree of typed operations.
note: Completed refers to the expression-tree exercise. The archive does not establish a finished generative-art application or gallery.
technical: Algebraic data types make each operation explicit. A structural recursion handles leaves directly and derives a parent’s depth from the deepest child.

implementation.use: Represent coordinates and operations as typed constructors.
Calculate expression depth from the deepest child.
Work through construction and inspection of compound expressions.

takeaway: A typed tree turns an image formula into inspectable structure. Recursive traversal supports composition and measures its depth.

title: Neural-network training notebooks
headline: Good models start with good data.
summary: PyTorch training exercises connect preprocessing, tensor shapes, loss functions and validation—the foundation for my later energy-inference work.
label: training and evaluation workflow
problem: A model cannot learn reliably when labels, tensor dimensions or preprocessing disagree. These exercises focused on constructing the complete training path rather than choosing a larger architecture.
approach: I worked on a simple convolutional network and a separate tabular classification notebook, connecting model outputs to loss calculation and optimizer updates.
I debugged dataset paths, numeric types, categorical preprocessing and validation predictions, checking how tensors move through the model.
result: Developed training and validation exercises that established the foundation for later spiking-network and energy-inference work.
Practiced tracing problems through preprocessing, model implementation and validation instead of judging a model from its training loss alone.
note: No validated accuracy gain is claimed. The CNN and tabular notebook are separate coursework exercises.
technical: Class-index labels and floating-point features have different type requirements. Validation should avoid gradient tracking and use the same fitted preprocessing as training.

implementation.use: Prepare tabular data and debug notebook input paths.
Connect model outputs, loss computation and parameter updates.
Check predictions without tracking gradients.

takeaway: The training loop is a chain of contracts between data, tensors, loss and validation. These exercises established the debugging habits behind my later ML deployments.
